details: No PII redaction, prompt-injection detector, or hallucination scorer ships. Section 16.1 calls it "BYO" via BeforeModelCallback / AfterModelCallback. Engineer is responsible for sourcing and wiring all guardrails.

First-class BaseGuardrail interface with three shipped guardrails: PromptInjectionGuardrail, PIIDetectionGuardrail, and OpenAIModerationGuardrail wired via pre_hooks/post_hooks. Raises InputCheckError / OutputCheckError. Directly matches the benchmark's first-party filter expectation.

autoagents-guardrails crate ships prompt_injection, regex_pii_redaction, and toxicity guards with Block/Sanitize/Audit policies and an LLMLayer integration. GuardrailBlocked errors propagate through the executor. Among the strongest first-party guardrail offerings.
Section 16.1 marks it red: no PII redaction, no prompt-injection detection, no hallucination detection. Must be built via UserPromptSubmit / PostToolUse hooks. No detector primitives shipped.

Not first-party; PII redaction / prompt-injection / hallucination detection are explicitly BYO via PreToolUse / PostToolUse hooks. No built-in detectors. Sandbox primitives are strong but guardrails are not.

Agent.guardrail and Task.guardrail callables run on output with retry, and LLMGuardrail*Event events stream. Built-in HallucinationGuardrail and PII redaction are AMP-only (paid). OSS provides the framework but ships no detectors.
Not first-party. PII / prompt-injection / hallucination detection are BYO via ChatModelAgentMiddleware that runs regex/classifier/LLM-judge. No shipped detectors.
Not provided as a first-party primitive in go/. Must scrub via WrapGenerate or reject in WrapTool. No shipped detectors.

Not provided — BYO. PII redaction, prompt-injection detection, hallucination detection live outside OSS runtime. Common patterns use pre_model_hook with Lakera/Presidio/OpenAI moderation wired as callbacks.
Not first-party in core. llama-index-integrations ecosystem includes llama-index-guardrails on PyPI and Guardrails AI / NeMo Guardrails integrations. Available but not shipped in core.

Built-in processors under packages/core/src/processors/processors/: moderation, pii-detector, prompt-injection-detector, cost-guard, regex-filter, language-detector, unicode-normalizer, system-prompt-scrubber. Each can ctx.abort with retry. Best-in-class first-party coverage.

Information-flow control via IntegrityLabel/ConfidentialityLabel/ContentLabel and LabelTrackingFunctionMiddleware / PolicyEnforcementFunctionMiddleware (ADR 0024). Purview integration package for Microsoft compliance labels. PII redaction remains BYO via middleware.

Best guardrail surface in the comparison: @input_guardrail, @output_guardrail, @tool_input_guardrail, @tool_output_guardrail with allow/reject_content/raise_exception tri-state. Tripwire mechanism halts runs. No shipped PII / prompt-injection detector — only the framework hooks.

First-class: InputGuardrail, OutputGuardrail, ToolInputGuardrail, ToolOutputGuardrail, HandoffEnabledPredicate. All produce tripwireTriggered halts. No first-party PII / prompt-injection detector — BYO via LlmGuard/Lakera.

First-party hooks (before_model_request, after_tool_execute, wrap_output_validate) let you plug detectors in. No bundled PII / injection detector. Third-party pydantic-ai-backend provides DockerSandbox.
Not provided. No built-in PII redaction, prompt-injection detection, or hallucination check. Pure BYO.

Bedrock Guardrails are first-class for the Bedrock provider: GuardrailConfig wired through, with redactContent chunks rewriting messages. Provider-specific only — for other providers it is BYO via hooks.
BedrockGuardrailConfig native plus a generic interventions subsystem with proceed/deny/guide/confirm/transform policy actions. GuardContentBlock support. PII / prompt-injection detection remains BYO.
Not provided. PII, prompt-injection, hallucination detection are BYO via LanguageModelMiddleware.transformParams or prepareStep. No shipped detectors.

No allow/deny list, no canUseTool hook. tool.FilterToolset removes tools from the LLM's view but tools that ARE in the toolset run as plain Go calls without sandbox. RequireConfirmation flag offers HITL gating only.

@tool(requires_confirmation=True) per-tool HITL gate, tool_hooks server-side deny, skills frontmatter allowed-tools, path-traversal protections in skill loaders, plus JWT-scope RBAC at the HTTP layer. Layered and composable.

AgentHooks::on_tool_call returning Abort gates per call. WasmRuntime executes tools in a wasmtime sandbox, and CodeActAgent runs TypeScript via Deno AST + rquickjs. No declarative per-tool allowlist data structure.

SandboxSettings (macOS sandbox-exec / Linux seccomp) with network allow/deny, excluded commands, ignore-violations, nested-sandbox. permission_mode default/acceptEdits/plan/bypassPermissions/dontAsk/auto plus can_use_tool callback. Most comprehensive permission surface in the comparison.

Section calls it "excellent": canUseTool callback, PreToolUse hook with allow/deny/defer, PermissionMode (six modes), PermissionRequest hook, persisted PermissionUpdate rules, per-MCP-server tool ACL, disallowedTools, tools: [] disable. The richest permission model.

Construction-time tools=[...] allow list, per-tool max_usage_count cap, before_tool_call hook returning False blocks, MCP ToolFilter. RBAC is AMP-only. No declarative per-tool ACL with role/group/scope rules in OSS.

Allow/deny via BeforeAgent middleware filtering runCtx.Tools is BYO. WrapInvokableToolCall returning an error denies a call. Per-tool ACL is also BYO. No built-in execution sandbox; tools run with the process's OS permissions.

ToolApproval middleware with AllowedTools allowlist interrupts on un-allowed tools requiring RestartWith approval. Filesystem middleware uses os.Root sandbox to block path escape via .. / abs paths / symlinks with size caps. Two real primitives but bash etc. unmanaged.
wrap_tool_call is the per-tool ACL hook returning a ToolMessage to deny. No declarative allow_tools=[...] list; engineers wire policy in the wrapper. Functional but everything is wrapper logic.
No canUseTool hook. Permission enforced only by what tools you put in tools=[...] at construction. Inside a tool you can raise to refuse, but no declarative ACL.

activeTools per-call whitelist, requireApproval boolean / needsApprovalFn per tool, RBAC + FGA at the HTTP layer with agents:execute/read perms, processInputStep returning {activeTools} as canUseTool equivalent. No direct canUseTool callback.

approval_mode ("always_require" / "never_require") on FunctionTool / @tool decorator (ADR 0006). ToolApprovalAgent in .NET tracks standing-approval rules / state. ContextProvider filters tools; FunctionMiddleware can terminate disallowed calls.

function_tool(needs_approval=True | callable) HITL with ToolApprovalItem and RunState.approve/reject, MCP server-level require_approval, 4 tool-level guardrail decorators, is_enabled per tool. No declarative allow/deny list but building blocks compose to the same effect.

tool({needsApproval: true | predicate}) runtime approval gate, tool({isEnabled}) visibility filter, per-tool inputGuardrails/outputGuardrails block or mutate, agent.toolUseBehavior limits loops. Strong layered approach.

@agent.tool(requires_approval=True) plus HandleDeferredToolCalls capability for HITL approval. before_tool_execute hook returning SkipToolExecution(result) gates calls. PrepareTools capability for per-step ACL and ApprovalRequiredToolset for declarative per-tool ACL.

Entire permission model is the on_tool_call hook returning Skip{reason} or Terminate. No per-tool ACL, no structured permission verdicts, no default-deny mode. Filtering is opt-in via hook logic only.

Permission enforced via BeforeToolCallEvent.cancel_tool (True or string) plus the Interrupt mechanism for HITL approval. No declarative allow-list; caller is responsible for python_repl / shell sandboxing.
Permission via BeforeToolCallEvent.cancel or InterventionHandler.beforeToolCall returning deny(reason). No declarative allowed_tools list at the agent config layer — you write the policy.

toolApproval returns approved/denied/user-approval per tool or globally with structured tool-output-denied chunks. activeTools allowlist filter, tool.needsApproval per-tool flag. Strong runtime gating.
No E2B, Daytona, Modal, or code-interpreter integration. Gemini's native code_execution runs in Google's sandbox but is opaque to the caller.
E2B, Daytona, and Docker tools all run code in remote/isolated sandboxes under tools/e2b.py, tools/daytona.py, tools/docker.py. Three first-party adapters.
No integrations with E2B / Daytona / Modal. AutoAgents brings its own sandbox (wasmtime + rquickjs) — in-tree but no external provider integrations.
First-party bash sandbox via OS primitives only (macOS sandbox-exec, Linux seccomp). No E2B / Daytona / Modal adapters.

Built-in Linux sandbox via bubblewrap configured by Options.sandbox SandboxSettings with filesystem/network restriction, allowUnixSockets, failIfUnavailable. Linux-only. No E2B / Daytona / Modal integration.

E2B and Daytona are first-party in crewai-tools. E2BBaseTool with E2BExecTool, E2BFileTool, E2BPythonTool across three lifecycle modes (one-shot, persistent, attach). DaytonaSandboxTool with similar shape.

eino-ext ships filesystem.Backend implementations: adk/backend/agentkit/ is a Docker-shelled Python interpreter (filesystem analog of E2B/Daytona, but only for the filesystem middleware). No E2B / Daytona / Modal direct integration.
No E2B, Daytona, Modal, or code-interpreter plugin in go/. googlegenai/code_execution exposes Gemini's built-in code execution as a model feature, not a Genkit-level sandbox.
Not in this repo. Engineers wire E2B / Daytona / Modal as @tool-decorated wrappers around their SDKs.

llama-index-tools-code-interpreter (local, not sandboxed), llama-index-tools-azure-code-interpreter (Azure hosted sandbox), llama-index-tools-aws-bedrock-agentcore. E2B / Daytona / Modal: no first-party packages found.
Not first-party. You bring your own (E2B, Daytona, Modal) and wrap in a createTool.

Hyperlight (Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hyperlight) hardware-isolated Wasm sandbox and DockerShellExecutor with ContainerUser / DockerNetworkMode / ShellPolicy for sandboxed shell execution. Strong first-party isolation choices.

Best in class: src/agents/extensions/sandbox/ ships blaxel, cloudflare, daytona, e2b, modal, runloop, vercel adapters. Each provider has mounts.py + sandbox.py exposing a BaseSandboxClient. Plus agents.computer.AsyncComputer for computer-use sandboxes.

Built-in UnixLocalSandboxClient (@openai/agents/sandbox/local) and OpenAI-hosted shell with container_auto. Third-party Docker / Blaxel / E2B-like providers referenced in CHANGELOG. Growing but smaller than Python sibling.
Third-party pydantic-ai-backend (Docker), various community packages. No E2B / Daytona / Modal integration in core.
Not provided. No E2B, Daytona, or Modal integration.
strands-agents-tools/code_interpreter/ ships sandbox bindings. Smaller surface than crewai/agno/openai-agents-python but present and first-party.
Not provided. The bash tool runs in-process; you sandbox at the OS / container level.

Experimental_Sandbox interface in @ai-sdk/provider-utils abstracts the runtime that hosts tool execution; tools receive options.experimental_sandbox. Concrete E2B / Daytona / Modal adapters are not first-party — you implement the interface.
Any tool placed on llmagent.Config.Tools or Toolsets is callable by the LLM. There is no policy layer to flip the posture.

Default-allow at tool registration (you ship the catalog), then deny via tool_hooks / guardrails / RBAC. JWT auth at the HTTP layer is deny-by-default when os_security_key or JWT is configured. Mixed posture.
AgentHooks::on_tool_call defaults to Continue. There is no central ACL — hook logic is the only gate.

permission_mode="default" prompts on dangerous tools; "dontAsk" is a true default-deny posture (only pre-approved tools run); bypassPermissions is default-allow. can_use_tool callback enables fine-grained control. Both postures available as first-class config.

permissionMode default prompts for dangerous operations from a CLI-defined exhaustive list. dontAsk flips to default-deny (only pre-approved tools run). Production typically uses acceptEdits or bypassPermissions with canUseTool gating. First-class posture toggle.

Tools are default-deny — an agent has only the tools you pass via tools=[...]. Skills default-deny similarly. MCP is default-allow (all server tools available unless ToolFilter set). Hooks default-allow. Mixed posture by subsystem.
All registered tools are visible to the LLM unless explicitly filtered. Skill middleware enumerates all skills by default. No allowTool gate before LLM can call it.
Default-allow for tools — everything registered is callable. ToolApproval middleware flips this to default-deny + explicit allowlist or approval, but it is opt-in per-call. No global toggle.
Default-allow. Whatever tools you pass to ToolNode / create_react_agent are dispatched. wrap_tool_call is opt-in for tightening — no built-in deny-first mode.
Default-allow. Whatever you pass to tools=[...] is callable. No deny-first posture toggle.
Default-deny for HTTP routes when server.auth is configured. Default-allow for tools unless requireApproval or activeTools whitelist is set. Mixed posture across layers.
Tools are default-allow (approval_mode defaults to "never_require"). Shell tools default to a ShellPolicy that denies unless explicitly allowed. Mixed posture per tool family.

Default-allow for tools — any tool in Agent(tools=[...]) is callable. Opt-in via needs_approval=True and guardrail decorators. Shell sandboxes ship explicit deny-network policies (ShellToolContainerNetworkPolicyAllowlist default-deny + allowlist). No global default-deny mode.
Tools default to isEnabled: true, needsApproval: false. The default is allow. Opt-in to deny via needsApproval predicate or isEnabled false.
Default-allow for declared tools, default-deny for unknown tools (model can only call registered ones). Approval is opt-in per tool via ApprovalRequiredToolset.
Default is allow-all-registered — every tool you .tool(...) is callable. Filtering is opt-in via hook logic. No default-deny mode.
Default-allow. python_repl and shell ship with confirmation prompts, but the SDK does not enforce an allow-list otherwise. Caller is responsible for tightening.
Default-allow. No tool requires explicit permission; the model can call any registered tool unless you intercept via hook.

Default-allow at tool dispatch — if toolApproval is not set, tools execute. Setting a global toolApproval: () => 'user-approval' cleanly flips the entire run to default-deny-pending-human. Easy one-line posture flip.
